claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on MSL1 protein interactions.

claims.claim: MSL1 and MSL2 form the structural core of the MSL complex.
claims.source: MSL1 and MSL2 form the structural core of the complex, whereas MLE—an ATP-dependent RNA/DNA helicase belonging to the DEAD box family—interacts with the roX1 and roX2 RNAs to induce their unwinding (Ilik et al., 2017; Maenner et al., 2013; Meller et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on MSL complex structure.

claims.claim: MLE is an ATP-dependent RNA/DNA helicase belonging to the DEAD box family that interacts with roX1 and roX2 RNAs to induce their unwinding.
claims.source: MSL1 and MSL2 form the structural core of the complex, whereas MLE—an ATP-dependent RNA/DNA helicase belonging to the DEAD box family—interacts with the roX1 and roX2 RNAs to induce their unwinding (Ilik et al., 2017; Maenner et al., 2013; Meller et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on MLE function.

claims.claim: The interaction of MLE with roX RNAs allows both RNAs to bind MSL2 and possibly MSL1, combining MLE, MSL2, and other MSL proteins into a single complex.
claims.source: This interaction allows both RNAs to bind MSL2 and possibly MSL1 (Müller et al., 2020), combining MLE, MSL2, and other MSL proteins into a single complex.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to literature on MSL complex assembly.

claims.claim: MOF forms the catalytic core of the nonspecific lethal complex (NSL), which is recruited to promoters on all chromosomes of both sexes and is responsible for strong transcriptional activation.
claims.source: In addition to the MSL complex, lysine acetyltransferase MOF forms the catalytic core of the nonspecific lethal complex (NSL), which is recruited to promoters located on all chromosomes of both sexes and is responsible for strong transcriptional activation (Sheikh et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to literature on the NSL complex.

claims.claim: In the MSL complex, MOF moderately stimulates transcription during RNA polymerase II elongation.
claims.source: Unlike the MSL complex, in which MOF moderately stimulates transcription during RNA polymerase II elongation (Ferrari et al., 2014; Kuroda et al., 2016), the NSL complex strongly increases the transcription at the initiation step (Sheikh et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on MOF function in the MSL complex.

claims.claim: The NSL complex strongly increases transcription at the initiation step.
claims.source: Unlike the MSL complex, in which MOF moderately stimulates transcription during RNA polymerase II elongation (Ferrari et al., 2014; Kuroda et al., 2016), the NSL complex strongly increases the transcription at the initiation step (Sheikh et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to literature on the NSL complex.

claims.claim: In males, formation of the MSL complex titrates MOF from the NSL complex, resulting in a decrease in its activity at all promoters.
claims.source: In males, formation of the MSL complex titrates MOF from the NSL complex, resulting in a decrease in its activity at all promoters (Prestel et al., 2010; Sun et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on MOF distribution.

claims.claim: Titration of MOF from the NSL complex may be one of the reasons for the inverse dose effect, which consists of a decrease in the expression of autosomal genes.
claims.source: This may be one of the reasons for the inverse dose effect, which consists of a decrease in the expression of autosomal genes (Birchler and Veitia, 2021).
claims.evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to literature on dosage compensation mechanisms.

claims.claim: An incomplete MSL1-MSL2 subcomplex can bind to a reproducible set of several hundreds of sites on the X chromosome, referred to as primary chromatin entry sites (CESs) or HAS.
claims.source: An incomplete MSL1-MSL2 subcomplex can bind to a reproducible set of several hundreds of sites on the X chromosome, referred to as the primary chromatin entry sites (CESs) (Alekseyenko et al., 2008) or HAS (Straub et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to literature identifying these sites.

claims.claim: A GA-rich motif within the HAS/CES, which serves as an MSL recognition element (MRE), is important for the MSL complex targeting.
claims.source: A GA-rich motif within the HAS/CES, which serves as an MSL recognition element (MRE), is important for the MSL complex targeting (Alekseyenko et al., 2008; Straub et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on MSL targeting sequences.

claims.claim: MSL2, through its CXC and proline/basic-residue-rich domains, specifically recognizes and binds to a subclass of HAS named pioneering sites on the X (PionX).
claims.source: Structural analysis and an in vitro genome-wide DNA binding assay showed that MSL2, through its CXC and proline/basic-residue-rich domains, specifically recognizes and binds to a subclass of HAS-named pioneering sites on the X (PionX) (Fauth et al., 2010; Villa et al., 2016; Zheng et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on MSL2 DNA binding.

claims.claim: CLAMP is a zinc-finger protein significant for the specific recruitment of the MSL complex to the male X chromosome.
claims.source: The zinc-finger protein chromatin-linked adaptor for MSL proteins (CLAMP) was found to be significant for the specific recruitment of the MSL complex to the male X chromosome (Eggers et al., 2023; Larschan et al., 2012; Soruco et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on CLAMP function.

claims.claim: CLAMP is an essential protein in Drosophila that binds thousands of GA-rich sequences genome-wide in both sexes.
claims.source: CLAMP is an essential protein in Drosophila that binds thousands of GA-rich sequences genome-wide in both sexes (Kuzu et al., 2016; Soruco et al., 2013; Urban et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on CLAMP binding.

claims.claim: CLAMP binds to GA repeats in HAS and is involved in the organization of open chromatin in these genome regions.
claims.source: In particular, CLAMP binds to GA repeats in HAS and is involved in the organization of open chromatin in these genome regions (Albig et al., 2019; Urban et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on CLAMP function in chromatin organization.

claims.claim: CLAMP has an N-terminal unstructured dimerization domain.
claims.source: CLAMP has an N-terminal unstructured dimerization domain (Tikhonova et al., 2022a) and promotes long-range chromatin interactions that mediate the dosage compensation of the male X chromosome (Jordan and Larschan, 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to literature on CLAMP structure.

claims.claim: CLAMP promotes long-range chromatin interactions that mediate the dosage compensation of the male X chromosome.
claims.source: CLAMP has an N-terminal unstructured dimerization domain (Tikhonova et al., 2022a) and promotes long-range chromatin interactions that mediate the dosage compensation of the male X chromosome (Jordan and Larschan, 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to literature on CLAMP function.

claims.claim: CLAMP directly interacts with the MSL2 protein.
claims.source: CLAMP also directly interacts with the MSL2 (Albig et al., 2019; Eggers et al., 2023; Tikhonova et al., 2022b; Tikhonova et al., 2019) and MLE (Quinn et al., 2014; Tikhonova et al., 2024) proteins.
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to literature on CLAMP-MSL2 interactions.

claims.claim: CLAMP directly interacts with the MLE protein.
claims.source: CLAMP also directly interacts with the MSL2 (Albig et al., 2019; Eggers et al., 2023; Tikhonova et al., 2022b; Tikhonova et al., 2019) and MLE (Quinn et al., 2014; Tikhonova et al., 2024) proteins.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on CLAMP-MLE interactions.

claims.claim: The CLAMP interaction and CXC domains of MSL2 have partially redundant functions for the recruitment of the MSL complex to the X chromosome.
claims.source: The CLAMP interaction and CXC domains of MSL2 have partially redundant functions for the recruitment of the MSL complex to the X chromosome (Tikhonova et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to literature on MSL2 recruitment mechanisms.

claims.claim: The N-terminal 265 amino acids region of MSL1 could bind to approximately 30 sites on polytene X chromosomes in females that exogenously express MSL2.
claims.source: A previous study (Li et al., 2005) showed that the N-terminal 265 amino acids region of MSL1 could bind to approximately 30 sites on polytene X chromosomes in females that exogenously express MSL2, and the first 26 aa are essential for such binding.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: The first 26 amino acids of MSL1 are essential for binding to polytene X chromosomes in females expressing MSL2.
claims.source: A previous study (Li et al., 2005) showed that the N-terminal 265 amino acids region of MSL1 could bind to approximately 30 sites on polytene X chromosomes in females that exogenously express MSL2, and the first 26 aa are essential for such binding.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: The N-terminal sequences of MSL1 can bind to DNA and facilitate the specific recruitment of MSL to the male X chromosome.
claims.source: The authors suggested that the N-terminal sequences of MSL1 can bind to DNA and facilitate the specific recruitment of MSL to the male X chromosome.
claims.evidence: This is a suggestion from a previous study cited in the manuscript.

claims.claim: MSL1 represents a core protein of the MSL complex.
claims.source: Although MSL1 represents a core protein of the MSL complex (Gorman et al., 1993; Palmer et al., 1993; Scott et al., 2000), MSL1 can also independently interact with gene promoters (Chlamydas et al., 2016, p. 2; Straub et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on MSL1 function.

claims.claim: MSL1 can independently interact with gene promoters.
claims.source: Although MSL1 represents a core protein of the MSL complex (Gorman et al., 1993; Palmer et al., 1993; Scott et al., 2000), MSL1 can also independently interact with gene promoters (Chlamydas et al., 2016, p. 2; Straub et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on MSL1 binding.

claims.claim: Deletion of the 1–15 amino acids of MSL1 results in the instability of MSL1.
claims.source: Deletion of the 1–15 aa results in the instability of MSL1.
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 1C showing loss of MSL1Δ1-15 protein.

claims.claim: The simultaneous replacement from 3 to 7 amino acids from the N-terminus of MSL1 strongly influences the binding of the MSL complex on the male X chromosome.
claims.source: Unexpectedly, we found that the simultaneous replacement from 3 to 7 aa from the N-terminus or deletion from 41 to 65 aa of MSL1 strongly influences the binding of the MSL complex on the male X chromosome.
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq and immunostaining data showing reduced MSL binding in MSL1GS mutants.

claims.claim: Deletion from 41 to 65 amino acids of MSL1 strongly influences the binding of the MSL complex on the male X chromosome.
claims.source: Unexpectedly, we found that the simultaneous replacement from 3 to 7 aa from the N-terminus or deletion from 41 to 65 aa of MSL1 strongly influences the binding of the MSL complex on the male X chromosome.
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq and immunostaining data showing reduced MSL binding in MSL1Δ41-65 mutants.

claims.claim: Mutations in the N-terminal region of MSL1 affect the interaction of MSL1 with roX2 RNA.
claims.source: These mutations also affect the interaction of MSL1 with roX2 RNA.
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA immunoprecipitation data in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: The N-terminal region of MSL1 performs key functions in the recruitment of the MSL complex to the X chromosome.
claims.source: Thus, the N-terminal region of MSL1 performs key functions in the recruitment of the MSL complex to the X chromosome.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on MSL1 mutants.

claims.claim: The first 15 amino acids represent the most conserved region within the N-terminus of MSL1 among Drosophilidae.
claims.source: With the exception of the coiled-coil domain, the first 15 amino acids represent the most conserved region within the N-terminus of MSL1 among Drosophilidae (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the sequence alignment shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Among different families of Diptera, a high level of homology was only observed for the coiled-coil region of MSL1.
claims.source: However, among different families of Diptera (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), a high level of homology was only observed for the coiled-coil region, which is required for interactions with MSL2 (Hallacli et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the sequence alignment in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and a citation.

claims.claim: The N-terminal amino acids of MSL1 are conserved among representatives within each of the Diptera families, but not across families.
claims.source: The N-terminal amino acids are also conserved among representatives within each of the Diptera families (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), but not across families.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the sequence alignment in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The MSL1 of Anopheles mosquitoes features a completely different N-terminal domain compared to Drosophila melanogaster.
claims.source: For example, the MSL1 of Anopheles mosquitoes, which are closely related to Drosophila melanogaster, features a completely different N-terminal domain.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the sequence alignment data.

claims.claim: MSL1 is expressed 2.5–3 times stronger under the control of the Ubi promoter in the transgenic line than in wild-type males.
claims.source: MSL1 is expressed 2.5–3 times stronger under the control of the Ubi promoter in the transgenic line than in wild-type males (y1w1118 line) (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claims.claim: Increased expression of MSL1 leads to the appearance of more MSL2, which is stabilized in a complex with MSL1.
claims.source: Increased expression of MSL1 leads to the appearance of more MSL2, which is stabilized in a complex with MSL1.
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data showing increased MSL2 levels with MSL1 overexpression.

claims.claim: In the absence of MSL2, the expression of MSL1 was lower in females compared to males.
claims.source: In the absence of MSL2, the expression of MSL1 was lower in females compared to males (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: MSL1Δ1-85 and MSL1Δ1-15 could not be detected by immunoblotting, suggesting the instability of these MSL1 variants.
claims.source: Immunoblot analysis showed that all MSL1 variants, with the exception of MSL1Δ1-85 and MSL1Δ1-15, were expressed in transgenic females at nearly equivalent levels (Figure 1C). Surprisingly, MSL1Δ1-85 and MSL1Δ1-15 could not be detected by immunoblotting, suggesting the instability of these MSL1 variants.
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: Homozygous msl-1− females remained viable, whereas males died during the late larva and early pupa stages.
claims.source: Homozygous msl-1− females remained viable, whereas males died during the late larva and early pupa stages (Gorman et al., 1993; Palmer et al., 1993).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on msl-1 mutant phenotypes.

claims.claim: The transgenes expressing MSL1WT and MSL1Δ66-85 compensated for the viability of msl-1− males.
claims.source: The transgenes, expressed MSL1WT and MSL1Δ66-85, compensated for the viability of msl-1− males, indicating that these MSL1 variants are functional (Figure 1D, Figure 1—source data 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by viability data in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: In MSL1Δ24-39 and MSL1Δ8-20 lines, male viability was reduced suggesting that dosage compensation is partially affected.
claims.source: In MSL1Δ24-39 and MSL1Δ8-20 lines, male viability was reduced suggesting that dosage compensation is partially affected.
claims.evidence: This is supported by viability data in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: MSL1Δ1-15, MSL1Δ1-85, MSL1Δ41-65, and MSL1Δ41-85 failed to compensate for the msl-1− mutation in males.
claims.source: In the end, all other tested mutant MSL1 proteins (MSL1Δ1-15, MSL1Δ1-85, MSL1Δ41-65, and MSL1Δ41-85) failed to compensate for the msl-1− mutation in males (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by viability data in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: At least two regions (1–15 aa and 41–65 aa) in the N-terminus of MSL1 are critical for the functional activity of the MSL complex.
claims.source: Taken together, these results suggested that at least two regions (1–15 aa and 41–65 aa) in the N-terminus of MSL1 are critical for the functional activity of the MSL complex.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the viability and expression data.

claims.claim: The amount of MSL1 was almost completely eliminated in females expressed either MSL1Δ1-15 and MSL2, or MSL1Δ1-85 and MSL2.
claims.source: Again, immunoblotting showed that the amount of MSL1 was almost completely eliminated in females expressed either MSL1Δ1-15 and MSL2, or MSL1Δ1-85 and MSL2 (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: There is no noticeable difference in the amount of MSL2 in all samples expressing different MSL1 variants.
claims.source: Interestingly, there is no noticeable difference in the amount of MSL2 in all samples.
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: The N-terminal 1–15 aa is essential for the stability of MSL1 independently of MSL2 presence.
claims.source: Thus, the N-terminal 1–15 aa is essential for the stability of MSL1 independently of MSL2 presence.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the immunoblot data showing MSL1 instability in the absence of the 1-15 aa region.

claims.claim: MSL1 and MSL2 were specifically recruited to the X chromosome in transgenic females expressing MSL2WT-FLAG under the control of the Ubi promoter.
claims.source: It was shown (Tikhonova et al., 2019), that MSL1 and MSL2 were specifically recruited to the X chromosome in transgenic females expressing MSL2WT-FLAG under the control of the Ubi promoter inserted into attP-line 86Fb (Ubi:msl-2WT-FLAG).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: When MSL2WT-FLAG was expressed in the msl-1− background, the binding of the MSL complex to the female X chromosome was not observed.
claims.source: When the MSL2WT-FLAG was expressed in the msl-1− background, we did not observe the binding of the MSL complex to the female X chromosome (data not shown).
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from the study.

claims.claim: The binding of MSL1 and MSL2 to the X chromosome was detected in msl-1− females when MSL2WT-FLAG was expressed simultaneously with either MSL1WT or MSL1Δ66-85.
claims.source: However, the binding of MSL1 and MSL2 to the X chromosome was detected in msl-1− females when MSL2WT-FLAG was expressed simultaneously with either MSL1WT or MSL1Δ66-85 (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The 66–85-aa region is not essential for MSL1 function in dosage compensation.
claims.source: These results further supported that the 66–85-aa region is not essential for MSL1 function in dosage compensation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the binding and viability data for MSL1Δ66-85.

claims.claim: Expression of MSL1Δ1-15 and MSL1Δ1-85 resulted in the near-complete loss of the MSL complex binding to the X chromosome in females.
claims.source: The expression of all MSL1 variants with deletions of the first 15-aa region (MSL1Δ1-15 and MSL1Δ1-85) resulted in the near-complete loss of the MSL complex binding to the X chromosome in females (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Inactivation of MSL3, MLE, or roX RNAs resulted in the recruitment of the MSL complex to a small proportion of bands that correspond to the main HAS.
claims.source: Previous studies (Dahlsveen et al., 2006; Demakova et al., 2003; Lyman et al., 1997; Meller and Rattner, 2002; Palmer et al., 1994) showed that the inactivation of MSL3, MLE, or roX RNAs resulted in the recruitment of the MSL complex to a small proportion of bands that correspond to the main HAS, including regions of the roX1 (3 F) and roX2 (10 C) genes.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: In polytene chromosomes in the MSL1Δ1-15 and MSL1Δ1-85 lines, only two intense and several faint MSL1/MSL2 bands were found.
claims.source: In polytene chromosomes in the MSL1Δ1-15 and MSL1Δ1-85 lines, we found only two intense and several faint MSL1/MSL2 bands (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Additional MSL1/MSL2 bands were identified on the polytene autosomes in MSL1Δ1-15 and MSL1Δ1-85 lines, suggesting that the MSL proteins began to bind to lower affinity sites on autosomes.
claims.source: Interestingly, additional MSL1/MSL2 bands were identified on the polytene autosomes, suggesting that the MSL proteins began to bind to lower affinity sites on autosomes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The deletion of the N terminal 15 aa affects not only the stability of MSL1 but also the specificity of MSL binding to the X chromosome.
claims.source: Thus, the deletion of the N terminal 15 aa affects not only the stability of MSL1 but also the specificity of MSL binding to the X chromosome.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the binding data showing altered MSL localization.

claims.claim: The deletion of the 41–85 aa or 41–65 aa regions did not affect the stability of MSL1, but significantly reduced the binding of MSL proteins to the X chromosome.
claims.source: The deletion of the 41–85 aa or 41–65 aa regions did not affect the stability of MSL1, but at the same time significantly reduced the binding of MSL proteins to the X chromosome.
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblot and immunostaining data.

claims.claim: MSL1Δ41-85 and MSL2 bind to several bands on the X chromosome, many of which can also be identified as weak bands in the MSL1Δ1-15 and MSL1Δ1-85 lines.
claims.source: MSL1Δ41-85 and MSL2 bind to several bands on the X chromosome, many of which can also be identified as weak bands in the MSL1Δ1-15 and MSL1Δ1-85 lines (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data in Figure 2 and supplements.

claims.claim: The binding of the MSL complex to the X chromosome in MSL1 mutants was much weaker than previously suggested for a minimal MSL complex lacking either MSL3 or MLE.
claims.source: However, the binding of the MSL complex to the X chromosome in MSL1 mutants was much weaker than previously suggested for a minimal MSL complex lacking either MSL3 or MLE (Dahlsveen et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison to previous studies supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The 41–65-aa region is critical for MSL1 function.
claims.source: As the 66–85-aa deletion did not affect the activity of MSL1, we concluded that the 41–65-aa region is critical for MSL1 function.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the effects of different deletions.

claims.claim: Deletion of 24–39 aa only moderately affects the binding of the MSL2 and MSL1Δ24-39 proteins on polytene chromosomes.
claims.source: Deletion of 24–39 aa, which separates the 1–15 aa and 41–65 aa regions in MSL1, only moderately affects the binding of the MSL2 and MSL1Δ24-39 proteins on polytene chromosomes (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The 1–15 aa and 41–65 aa regions have at least partially independent functions in recruiting of the MSL complex to the X chromosome in males.
claims.source: This observation indicates that the 1–15 aa and 41–65 aa regions have at least partially independent functions in recruiting of the MSL complex to the X chromosome in males.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differential effects of deletions.

claims.claim: In MSL1Δ8-20 female larvae patterns of MSL1 and MSL2 binding to polytene chromosome are the same as in larvae expressed MSL1Δ24-39.
claims.source: In MSL1Δ8-20 female larvae patterns of MSL1 and MSL2 binding to polytene chromosome are the same as in larvae expressed MSL1Δ24-39 (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data in Figure 2 and supplements.

claims.claim: A deletion from 8 aa up to 20 aa only partially affects the functions of MSL1, in contrast to the complete inactivation of this protein by deleting the terminal 15 aa.
claims.source: Thus, a deletion from 8 aa up to 20 aa only partially affects the functions of MSL1, in contrast to the complete inactivation of this protein by deleting the terminal 15 aa (MSL1Δ1-15).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the effects of different deletions.

claims.claim: MSL1Δ1-15 is unstable, while MSL1Δ8-20 only partially affects the specific recruitment of MSL to the X chromosome.
claims.source: Our results showed that MSL1Δ1-15 is unstable, while MSL1Δ8-20 only partially affects the specific recruitment of MSL to the X chromosome suggesting that the most terminal amino-acids are essential for functions.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claims.claim: The N-terminal region contains well-conserved basic and aromatic amino acid residues.
claims.source: The N-terminal region contains well-conserved basic and aromatic amino acid residues (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the sequence alignment in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: MSL12A and MSL13S variants were expressed at levels comparable to MSL1WT in msl-1− females.
claims.source: MSL12A and MSL13S variants were expressed at levels comparable to MSL1WT in 2–3 day-old msl-1− females that are homozygous for the MSL1 transgenes (Figure 3B and C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 3B and C.

claims.claim: There was an approximately 1.5–2-fold decrease in the MSL1GS protein compared to MSL1WT.
claims.source: At the same time, there was an approximately 1.5–2-fold decrease in the MSL1GS protein compared to MSL1WT.
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data in Figure 3B and C.

claims.claim: The transgenes expressing MSL12A and MSL13S almost completely compensated for the viability of msl-1− males.
claims.source: The transgenes, expressed MSL12A and MSL13S, almost completely compensated for the viability of msl-1− males, indicating that these MSL1 variants are functional (Figure 3D, Figure 3—source data 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by viability data in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: In the msl-1− line expressing MSL1GS, the viability of males was strongly reduced.
claims.source: In the msl-1− line expressing MSL1GS, the viability of males was strongly reduced.
claims.evidence: This is supported by viability data in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Increasing MSL2 and a simultaneous decreasing in MSL1GS expression partially restore the viability of MSL1GS/MSL2 males.
claims.source: At the same time, increasing in MSL2 and a simultaneous decreasing in MSL1GS expression partially restore the viability of MSL1GS/MSL2 males (Figure 3E, Figure 3—source data 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by viability data in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: The viability of MSL1Δ8-20/MSL2 males is close to wild-type.
claims.source: In a similar way, the viability of MSL1Δ8-20/MSL2 males also is close to wild-type, but MSL1Δ41-65/MSL2 and MSL1Δ1-15/MSL2 males are still lethal.
claims.evidence: This is supported by viability data in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: MSL1Δ41-65/MSL2 and MSL1Δ1-15/MSL2 males are still lethal.
claims.source: In a similar way, the viability of MSL1Δ8-20/MSL2 males also is close to wild-type, but MSL1Δ41-65/MSL2 and MSL1Δ1-15/MSL2 males are still lethal.
claims.evidence: This is supported by viability data in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: MSL12A and MSL13S showed binding patterns like MSL1WT on the larva polytene chromosome.
claims.source: According to the results obtained on males, MSL12A and MSL13S showed binding patterns like MSL1WT on the larva polytene chromosome, while the MSL1GS protein failed to effectively bind on the X chromosome in complex with MSL2 (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data in Figure 3F and supplements.

claims.claim: The MSL1GS protein failed to effectively bind on the X chromosome in complex with MSL2.
claims.source: According to the results obtained on males, MSL12A and MSL13S showed binding patterns like MSL1WT on the larva polytene chromosome, while the MSL1GS protein failed to effectively bind on the X chromosome in complex with MSL2 (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data in Figure 3F and supplements.

claims.claim: There are binding sites for only MSL2 or MSL1GS on the autosomes and the X chromosome.
claims.source: There are also binding sites for only MSL2 or MSL1GS on the autosomes and the X chromosome.
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data in Figure 3F and supplements.

claims.claim: The N-terminal amino acids 3–7 additively contribute to specific recruitment of MSL on the X chromosome.

claims.claim: The significance of roX RNAs in specific MSL recruitment to the X chromosome remains an open question requiring further examination.
claims.source: However, for Drosophila, the significance of roX RNAs in specific MSL recruitment to the X chromosome remains an open question requiring further examination.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

results.result: The N-terminal 15 amino acids of MSL1 are highly conserved among Drosophilidae but not across different Diptera families, with each family showing distinct N-terminal sequences despite conservation of the coiled-coil domain.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C57 and C141-C142 are supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1. The conservation pattern within Drosophilidae and divergence across Diptera families is clearly demonstrated through comparative sequence analysis.

results.result: Deletion of the N-terminal 1-15 amino acids of MSL1 results in protein instability, with MSL1Δ1-15 being undetectable by immunoblotting in both flies and S2 cells, independent of MSL2 presence.
results.evaluation: Claims C49, C61, C67, C69, C102, and C135 are consistently supported by immunoblot data from Figures 1C, 1E, and 4A showing loss of MSL1Δ1-15 protein in multiple experimental contexts. The independence from MSL2 is demonstrated in Figure 1E.

results.result: Two regions in the N-terminus of MSL1 (amino acids 1-15 and 41-65) are critical for MSL complex function, as demonstrated by male viability assays showing that deletions in these regions fail to rescue msl-1− males while MSL1Δ66-85 remains functional.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C66 and C73 are supported by viability data in Figure 1D showing differential rescue of msl-1− males by various MSL1 deletion constructs. The functional importance of the 1-15 and 41-65 regions is clearly demonstrated through loss-of-function phenotypes.

results.result: MSL1Δ1-15 and MSL1Δ1-85 variants show near-complete loss of MSL complex binding to the X chromosome in females expressing MSL2, with only a few weak bands remaining and aberrant binding to autosomal sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C72, C74, C76-C78 are supported by immunostaining data in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplements 1-2 showing dramatically reduced X chromosome binding and ectopic autosomal binding in MSL1Δ1-15 and MSL1Δ1-85 lines.

results.result: Deletion of amino acids 41-65 in MSL1 does not affect protein stability but significantly reduces MSL complex binding to the X chromosome, with binding being weaker than previously reported for minimal MSL complexes lacking MSL3 or MLE.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C82 are supported by immunoblot data showing stable MSL1Δ41-65 protein (Figure 1C) combined with immunostaining data (Figure 2) showing reduced X chromosome binding. The comparison to previous studies (C81) is appropriately cited.

results.result: The 1-15 aa and 41-65 aa regions of MSL1 have partially independent functions in MSL complex recruitment, as demonstrated by the intermediate phenotypes of MSL1Δ24-39 and MSL1Δ8-20 deletions that separate or partially overlap these critical regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C87 are supported by immunostaining data in Figure 2 and viability data in Figure 1D showing that deletions in the linker region (24-39 aa) or partial deletions (8-20 aa) produce intermediate phenotypes, suggesting independent contributions of the two critical regions.

results.result: Substitution of N-terminal amino acids 3-7 (MSL1GS) slightly reduces protein stability and strongly impairs MSL complex binding to the X chromosome and male viability, while individual substitutions (MSL12A, MSL13S) have minimal effects, indicating additive contributions of these residues.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C92, C96-C97, and C99 are supported by immunoblot data (Figure 3B-C), viability assays (Figure 3D), and immunostaining (Figure 3F) showing that combined substitution of amino acids 3-7 produces severe defects while individual substitutions do not, demonstrating additive effects.

results.result: Overexpression of MSL2 partially restores viability in MSL1GS males and MSL1Δ8-20 males but not in MSL1Δ41-65 or MSL1Δ1-15 males, suggesting that increased MSL2 can partially compensate for impaired MSL1-roX interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C95, C9, and C167 are supported by viability data in Figure 3E showing differential rescue by MSL2 overexpression depending on the MSL1 mutation. The partial rescue of MSL1GS is consistent with the hypothesis that high MSL2 concentration can bypass some roX RNA requirements.

results.result: In S2 cells, MSL1GS and MSL1Δ41-85 can co-immunoprecipitate with MSL2 as efficiently as MSL1WT, suggesting these mutants can form complexes with MSL2, likely through heterodimerization with endogenous wild-type MSL1.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C101, C104-C105 are supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4B showing that MSL1GS and MSL1Δ41-85 interact with MSL2 in S2 cells. However, the interpretation that this occurs through heterodimerization with endogenous MSL1 (C106) is speculative and requires further validation.

results.result: MSL1GS and MSL1Δ41-85 can heterodimerize with wild-type MSL1 via the coiled-coil domain and enter functional MSL complexes that bind specifically to the male X chromosome when wild-type MSL1 is present, demonstrating that MSL1 dimerization does not require roX RNAs.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C108 and C169-C170 are supported by immunostaining data in Figure 4C showing co-localization of mutant and wild-type MSL1 on the X chromosome in heterozygous flies. This demonstrates functional heterodimerization and suggests roX RNAs are not required for MSL1 dimerization itself.

results.result: ChIP-seq analysis shows that MSL proteins bind to approximately 90% of previously identified HAS in adult males, with similar binding patterns in S2 cells, and that ectopic MSL2 expression in females is sufficient to trigger correct MSL complex targeting to the X chromosome.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C111 and C114 are supported by ChIP-seq data in Figure 5 and supplements showing high overlap with previously identified HAS and correlation between male and female+MSL2 binding patterns. The conclusion is consistent with cited prior work (C114).

results.result: MSL1Δ1-15, MSL1Δ41-85, and MSL1GS mutations strongly reduce MSL1, MSL2, and MSL3 binding to most X chromosomal HAS, but MSL2 continues to bind effectively to a subset of sites (Cluster 2) enriched for PionX sites, suggesting MSL2 can bind some sites independently.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C122 are supported by ChIP-seq data in Figures 5-6 showing reduced binding at most HAS but maintained MSL2 binding at PionX-enriched sites. Statistical analysis (Wilcoxon tests with significant p-values) supports the differential binding at PionX sites in mutants.

results.result: MSL1GS retains the ability to bind promoters independently of the MSL complex with the same efficiency as MSL1WT, while MSL1Δ1-15 and MSL1Δ41-85 do not bind these sites, suggesting the 41-85 aa region facilitates MSL1 interaction with promoter-associated transcription factors.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C127 are supported by ChIP-seq data analysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 2) showing differential binding of MSL1 variants at promoter sites where MSL2 is absent. The interpretation about the 41-85 aa region (C127) is a reasonable inference from the data.

results.result: RNA immunoprecipitation experiments demonstrate that MSL1WT interacts with roX2 RNA while MSL1GS and MSL1Δ41-85 do not, supporting the hypothesis that failure to interact with roX RNAs is the primary cause of functional inactivation of these mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C133 are supported by RT-qPCR data (Figure 7A) showing equal roX2 expression and RNA-IP data (Figure 7C) showing differential roX2 recovery with MSL1WT versus mutants. The conclusion that loss of roX interaction causes functional inactivation is well-supported by the combined functional and biochemical data.

results.result: The N-terminal region of MSL1, particularly amino acids 3-7 and 41-85, is critical for MSL1 stability, interaction with roX2 RNA, and efficient assembly of the MSL complex on HAS of the male X chromosome, with roX RNA accelerating the interaction of MSL2 with the MSL1 dimer.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C6, C10, C53, C136-C137, C162, C171, and C176 represent the main conclusions of the study and are well-supported by the comprehensive experimental data including viability assays, immunostaining, ChIP-seq, and RNA-IP experiments. The model is consistent with recent literature (cited in C176).

results.result: MSL1GS mutation affects male viability similar to roX RNA inactivation, with MSL1GS binding to promoters like MSL1WT but failing to co-bind with MSL2 and MSL3 to X chromosomal HAS, resulting in very low male viability comparable to roX- males.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C8, C163-C164 are supported by viability data (Figure 3D), ChIP-seq data (Figures 5-6), and comparison to published roX- phenotypes (cited). The parallel between MSL1GS and roX- phenotypes strengthens the conclusion about the importance of MSL1-roX interaction.

results.result: MSL1 is expressed 2.5-3 times more strongly under the Ubi promoter in transgenic lines than in wild-type males, leading to increased MSL2 levels through stabilization in complex with MSL1, with stronger MSL binding observed in transgenic males.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C60 and C112 are supported by immunoblot data (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A) and ChIP-seq data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, 2A). The overexpression is appropriately controlled for in the experimental design and interpretations.

results.result: Previous UV-XL studies showed that the N-terminal 191 aa of MSL1 and MSL2 are direct roX2 interactors, and given the functional redundancy of roX1 and roX2, roX1 likely interacts with the same N-terminal regions of MSL1.
results.evaluation: Claims C134, C128, C139-C140 appropriately cite prior work (Müller et al., 2020; Meller and Rattner, 2002; Stuckenholz et al., 2003) and make reasonable inferences about roX1 based on established redundancy. The inference about roX1 (C140) is logical but not directly tested.

results.result: The structure of human MSL1-MSL2 complex does not require RNA, but in Drosophila, MSL2 interacts with MSL1's coiled-coil domain via its RING finger, suggesting the Drosophila interaction may be weaker and require roX RNAs for efficient association.
results.evaluation: Claims C172-C175 cite relevant prior work but the speculation about weaker interaction in Drosophila (C174) is not directly tested in this study. While the data are consistent with this model, direct structural or biophysical comparison between human and Drosophila complexes would be needed for stronger support.

results.result: Background information on the MSL complex composition, function in dosage compensation, protein domains, interactions, and recruitment mechanisms including the roles of CLAMP, MRE, HAS, and PionX sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4, C11, C14-C43 represent established background knowledge appropriately cited from the literature. These claims provide context for the study but are not novel findings. All are well-supported by the cited references.

results.result: Background on the generally accepted model of MSL complex recruitment to HAS containing GAGA/MRE motifs, the role of CLAMP in chromatin opening, MSL2's recognition of HAS, and roX RNAs' role in guiding MSL complex assembly and spreading.
results.evaluation: Claims C144-C155 represent established models and mechanisms from the literature, appropriately cited. These provide important context for interpreting the current findings but are not novel results from this study.

results.result: Background on ongoing debates about dosage compensation mechanisms, evolutionary considerations of X chromosome formation, and comparisons to mammalian X inactivation via Xist, with acknowledgment that the significance of roX RNAs in MSL recruitment remains an open question.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C13, C143, C180-C182 appropriately cite literature on unresolved questions and evolutionary context. The acknowledgment of open questions (C182) is appropriate scientific caution. These are contextual rather than novel findings.

results.result: Previous work by Li et al. (2005) showed that the N-terminal 265 aa of MSL1 could bind to polytene X chromosomes in females expressing MSL2, with the first 26 aa being essential, and suggested that N-terminal sequences facilitate MSL recruitment, though MSL1 can also independently interact with promoters.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C48 appropriately cite and describe prior work that motivated the current study. The suggestion about DNA binding (C46) is noted as speculative from the prior work. These claims provide important historical context.

results.result: Background on msl-1 mutant phenotypes, previous observations about MSL complex binding in various mutant backgrounds, and MSL protein binding patterns at promoters independent of the full complex.
results.evaluation: Claims C62, C70-C71, C75, C123, C158, C160, C165-C166 cite relevant prior work that provides context for the experimental design and interpretation. These are appropriately referenced and provide important background.

results.result: Interpretive conclusions about the mechanisms of MSL1 stability, heterodimerization, the dual role of the 41-85 aa region, and the consequences of disrupted MSL complex formation, including speculation about MSL2 overexpression rescue mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C103, C106, C156-C157, C159, C161, C168, C177-C179 represent interpretations and inferences from the data. While generally reasonable, some (particularly C106, C168, C177) are speculative and would benefit from additional direct experimental validation. The inferences are logical but not definitively proven.

results.result: The N-terminal 1-15 amino acids of MSL1 are critical for protein stability. Deletion of this region (MSL1Δ1-15) results in complete loss of MSL1 protein detection by immunoblotting in both flies and S2 cells, independent of MSL2 presence.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged 'the deletion analysis of the MSL1 protein and the tests of interaction with MSL2 are adequate.' The immunoblot data showing loss of MSL1Δ1-15 protein (Figure 1C, 1E) and the conclusion about stability are not challenged by reviewers.

results.result: Amino acid substitutions (MSL1GS, residues 3-7) and deletions (41-65 aa) in the N-terminal region of MSL1 strongly affect both the interaction with roX2 RNA and MSL complex binding to HAS on the X chromosome. These mutations reduce male viability and disrupt dosage compensation.
results.evaluation: While reviewers found 'the deletion analysis of the MSL1 protein and the tests of interaction with MSL2 are adequate,' they explicitly stated that 'sex-specific viability is insufficient to make claims regarding dosage compensation' and that 'there are many ways to alter viability.' The RNA interaction data is not directly challenged, but the interpretation regarding dosage compensation is questioned.

results.result: Substitution of conserved N-terminal amino acids 3-7 in MSL1 (MSL1GS) affects male viability similar to inactivation of roX RNA genes, with males expressing MSL1GS showing very low viability comparable to roX- males.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly stated that 'sex-specific viability is insufficient to make claims regarding dosage compensation' and noted 'there are many ways to alter viability.' While the viability data itself is not disputed, the interpretation linking it to dosage compensation mechanisms is questioned.

results.result: MSL1GS binds to promoters like MSL1WT but does not co-bind with MSL2 and MSL3 to X chromosomal HAS. ChIP-seq data shows MSL1GS effectively binds to autosomal promoters but disrupts MSL complex recruitment to X chromosomal HAS.
results.evaluation: Reviewers stated 'the deletion analysis of the MSL1 protein and the tests of interaction with MSL2 are adequate.' The ChIP-seq data showing differential binding patterns is technical and not challenged by reviewers, who focused their critique on the interpretation of dosage compensation rather than the binding data itself.

results.result: Overexpression of MSL2 partially restores viability in MSL1GS mutant males, suggesting that high MSL2 concentration can partially compensate for the loss of MSL1-roX interaction.
results.evaluation: While the viability rescue data is not directly challenged, reviewers stated that 'sex-specific viability is insufficient to make claims regarding dosage compensation.' The mechanistic interpretation about compensating for MSL1-roX interaction loss is therefore uncertain given the reviewers' concerns about using viability as a readout for dosage compensation.

results.result: The interaction of MSL1 with roX RNA is critical for efficient assembly of the MSL complex on HAS of the male X chromosome. Failure to interact with roX RNAs is proposed as the primary cause of functional inactivation of MSL1GS and MSL1Δ41-85 mutants.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not directly challenge the RNA interaction data, stating 'the deletion analysis of the MSL1 protein and the tests of interaction with MSL2 are adequate.' However, the broader interpretation about MSL complex function in dosage compensation is questioned, as reviewers stated the 'framework that the MSL complex mediates dosage compensation is outdated and has flaws' and that 'the MSL complex is not the primary mediator of X chromosome dosage compensation.'

results.result: RNA immunoprecipitation experiments show that roX2 RNA is detected in precipitates from MSL1WT extracts but not from MSL1GS or MSL1Δ41-85 precipitates, demonstrating that MSL1WT interacts with roX2 while the mutants do not.
results.evaluation: Reviewers stated 'the deletion analysis of the MSL1 protein and the tests of interaction with MSL2 are adequate.' The RNA immunoprecipitation data (Figure 7C) is technical and not challenged by reviewers.

results.result: The MSL complex is involved in transcriptional enhancement of X-linked genes to compensate for sex chromosome monosomy in Drosophila males. Dosage compensation is achieved by doubling expression of genes on the single male X chromosome and may involve simultaneous activation of X chromosome transcription and inverse dosage effects on autosomes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly rejected this framework, stating 'the framework that the MSL complex mediates dosage compensation is outdated and has flaws' and 'the MSL complex is not the primary mediator of X chromosome dosage compensation.' They cite evidence that 'when the MSL complex is disrupted, there is no overall loss of compensation but there is an increase in autosomal expression' and that 'dosage compensation of the X chromosome can be robust in the absence of the MSL complex.'

results.result: In males, formation of the MSL complex titrates MOF from the NSL complex, resulting in decreased activity at all promoters. This titration may be one reason for the inverse dose effect, which consists of decreased expression of autosomal genes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly stated 'the authors state that an inverse dosage effect results from a titration of the histone acetylase MOF between the NSL and MSL complexes. This is a misunderstanding of the inverse effect, which is an imbalance of regulatory molecules.' They note 'the inverse effect operates in triple X metafemales to produce dosage compensation of the three X chromosomes and a reduced expression of the autosomes. There is no MSL complex in metafemales.'

results.result: The first 15 amino acids represent the most conserved region within the N-terminus of MSL1 among Drosophilidae. However, among different families of Diptera, high homology is only observed for the coiled-coil region, with N-terminal sequences differing across families.
results.evaluation: The sequence alignment data (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1) is descriptive and not challenged by reviewers. This is supporting information for the functional studies.

results.result: In S2 cells, MSL1WT and most mutant variants (MSL1Δ8-20, MSL1Δ24-39, MSL1Δ41-85, MSL12A, MSL13S, MSL1GS) are stable and co-immunoprecipitate with MSL2, while MSL1Δ1-15 and MSL1Δ1-85 are unstable. This confirms that specific N-terminal amino acid combinations are required for MSL1 stability.
results.evaluation: Reviewers stated 'the deletion analysis of the MSL1 protein and the tests of interaction with MSL2 are adequate.' The co-immunoprecipitation data in S2 cells (Figure 4B) is technical and not challenged.

results.result: In the presence of wild-type MSL1, MSL1GS and MSL1Δ41-85 variants enter the MSL complex and specifically bind to the male X chromosome through heterodimerization via the coiled-coil domain. This suggests efficient MSL1 dimerization does not require roX RNAs.
results.evaluation: Reviewers found 'the deletion analysis of the MSL1 protein and the tests of interaction with MSL2 are adequate.' The co-localization data (Figure 4C) showing rescue by wild-type MSL1 is not challenged.

results.result: ChIP-seq data from adult males shows MSL binding to approximately 90% of previously identified HAS. Most HAS are common between S2 cells and adult males. MSL2 expression in females induces MSL complex binding to the same HAS regions as in males, though with lower efficiency.
results.evaluation: The ChIP-seq data is technical and not directly challenged by reviewers. Reviewers stated 'the deletion analysis of the MSL1 protein and the tests of interaction with MSL2 are adequate,' which encompasses the binding studies.

results.result: Hierarchical clustering of HAS reveals two clusters: 'MSL2 Sensitive' sites where proteins do not bind during MSL1 mutant expression, and 'MSL2 stable' sites where MSL2 continues to bind even with MSL1 mutations. PionX sites are enriched in the MSL2 stable cluster, suggesting some PionX sites may be bound independently by MSL2.
results.evaluation: The ChIP-seq clustering analysis is technical and not challenged by reviewers. This represents detailed characterization of binding patterns that follows from the accepted deletion analysis.

results.result: Viability assays show that MSL1WT and MSL1Δ66-85 compensate for msl-1− male lethality, while MSL1Δ1-15, MSL1Δ1-85, MSL1Δ41-65, and MSL1Δ41-85 fail to rescue. MSL1Δ24-39 and MSL1Δ8-20 show reduced male viability. This suggests at least two regions (1-15 aa and 41-65 aa) are critical for MSL1 function with partially independent roles.
results.evaluation: While the viability data itself is not disputed, reviewers explicitly stated that 'sex-specific viability is insufficient to make claims regarding dosage compensation' and 'there are many ways to alter viability.' The interpretation that these regions are critical for 'dosage compensation' function is therefore uncertain.

results.result: Immunostaining of polytene chromosomes shows that MSL1WT and MSL1Δ66-85 bind to the X chromosome with MSL2, while deletions of 1-15 aa or 41-85 aa regions result in near-complete loss of X chromosome binding and appearance of autosomal binding sites. The 24-39 aa deletion moderately affects binding.
results.evaluation: Reviewers stated 'the deletion analysis of the MSL1 protein and the tests of interaction with MSL2 are adequate.' The immunostaining data on polytene chromosomes (Figure 2 and supplements) showing binding patterns is technical and not challenged.

results.result: Point mutation analysis shows MSL12A and MSL13S variants are expressed at levels comparable to MSL1WT, almost completely rescue male viability, and show normal X chromosome binding patterns. MSL1GS shows reduced expression and fails to bind effectively to the X chromosome, suggesting N-terminal amino acids 3-7 additively contribute to MSL recruitment.
results.evaluation: While reviewers found 'the deletion analysis of the MSL1 protein and the tests of interaction with MSL2 are adequate,' they stated 'sex-specific viability is insufficient to make claims regarding dosage compensation.' The binding data is not challenged, but the interpretation about dosage compensation function is uncertain.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement. Both evaluate sequence alignment data (C54-C57, C141-C142) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes conservation patterns demonstrated through comparative sequence analysis; peer reviewers find this descriptive data not challenged.

Strong agreement on protein stability data. Both find immunoblot evidence (C49, C61, C69, C135) SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes MSL1Δ1-15 protein loss across multiple contexts; peer reviewers acknowledge deletion analysis and MSL2 interaction tests are adequate.

Disagreement on interpretation. OpenEval finds viability data (C63-C66, C73) SUPPORTED for demonstrating functional importance; peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, stating 'sex-specific viability is insufficient to make claims regarding dosage compensation' and 'there are many ways to alter viability.'

Agreement on binding data. Both find immunostaining data (C72, C74, C76-C78) SUPPORTED showing reduced X chromosome binding and ectopic autosomal binding. Peer reviewers note deletion analysis is adequate; technical binding data not challenged.

Agreement on binding phenotypes. OpenEval finds C79-C82 SUPPORTED by combined immunoblot and immunostaining data; peer reviewers also find related binding data (C79-C81) SUPPORTED as part of adequate deletion analysis.

Partial disagreement. OpenEval finds intermediate phenotypes (C83-C87) SUPPORTED; peer reviewers rate overlapping claims (C84, C86, C87) as UNCERTAIN due to concerns about using viability as readout for dosage compensation function.

Disagreement on interpretation. OpenEval finds additive effects of substitutions (C89-C92, C96-C97, C99) SUPPORTED; peer reviewers rate overlapping claims (C89-C91, C96, C99) UNCERTAIN, stating viability data insufficient for dosage compensation claims despite adequate deletion analysis.

Disagreement on mechanistic interpretation. OpenEval finds MSL2 overexpression rescue data (C93-C95, C9, C167) SUPPORTED; peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, questioning whether viability rescue demonstrates compensation for roX RNA requirements given broader concerns about viability as dosage compensation readout.

Agreement on interaction data with caveats. Both find co-IP data (C100-C101, C104) SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes heterodimerization interpretation (C106) is speculative; peer reviewers find MSL2 interaction tests adequate without challenging the data.

Agreement on co-localization data. Both find immunostaining evidence (C107-C108, C169-C170) SUPPORTED showing functional heterodimerization. OpenEval and peer reviewers agree this demonstrates MSL1 dimerization independent of roX RNAs.

Agreement on ChIP-seq binding patterns. Both find data (C109-C111, C114) SUPPORTED showing overlap with HAS and correlation between binding patterns. Peer reviewers note technical ChIP-seq data not challenged; focus critique on interpretation rather than binding data.

Agreement on differential binding analysis. Both find ChIP-seq clustering data (C115-C122) SUPPORTED showing reduced binding at most HAS but maintained binding at PionX sites. Peer reviewers find technical characterization adequate.

Agreement on promoter binding patterns. OpenEval finds differential MSL1 variant binding (C124-C127) SUPPORTED; peer reviewers find overlapping ChIP-seq data (C124) SUPPORTED as part of adequate binding studies, not directly challenged.

Agreement on RNA interaction data. Both find RT-qPCR and RNA-IP data (C129-C133) SUPPORTED showing differential roX2 recovery. OpenEval emphasizes loss of roX interaction causes functional inactivation; peer reviewers find RNA interaction tests adequate.

Major disagreement on main conclusions. OpenEval finds comprehensive support for MSL1-roX interaction model (C5-C6, C10, C53, C136-C137, C162, C171, C176); peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, stating 'framework that MSL complex mediates dosage compensation is outdated' and questioning interpretation despite adequate technical data.

Disagreement on phenotype interpretation. OpenEval finds parallel between MSL1GS and roX- phenotypes (C7-C8, C163-C164) SUPPORTED; peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, stating viability data insufficient for dosage compensation claims despite not challenging the binding data.

Agreement on overexpression controls. Both find immunoblot and ChIP-seq data (C58-C60, C112) SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes appropriate experimental controls; peer reviewers find technical data adequate as part of binding studies.

Fundamental disagreement on framework. OpenEval finds main conclusions (C10, C162, C171, C176) well-SUPPORTED; peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, stating 'MSL complex is not the primary mediator of X chromosome dosage compensation' and that 'dosage compensation can be robust in absence of MSL complex.'

Fundamental disagreement on background framework. OpenEval finds established background (C1-C4, C11, C14-C43) SUPPORTED by literature; peer reviewers explicitly reject framework (C2, C11, C13, C14) as UNSUPPORTED, stating it is 'outdated and has flaws.'

Disagreement on mechanistic model. OpenEval finds established models (C144-C155) SUPPORTED as appropriate context; peer reviewers explicitly reject inverse dosage effect explanation (C31-C32) as UNSUPPORTED, stating 'this is a misunderstanding of the inverse effect.'
